nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What are the two types of stability associated with coalitions in IEAs?
nodes.answer: Internal stability (where signatories do not want to leave) and external stability (where non-signatories do not find it profitable to join).
nodes.paragraph: Moreover, all cooperators must voluntarily ratify the treaty and stay in the agreement, due to the absence of a supranational authority that could implement and enforce environmen- tal policies on sovereign countries. An IEA must use the interplay of incentives and interactions among agents to be self-enforcing. The freedom of entrance and depar - ture leads to questions about stability of IEAs. Different game theoretic strands of economic literature have studied the formation and stability of international environ- mental agreements. The non-cooperative approach uses a stability concept proposed by d Aspremont et al. (1983) in the study of cartels, in order to determine the size of a coalition. A coalition is considered to be stable if a signatory is not favourable to leave the agreement (internal stability) and if a non-signatory is not profitable to join the agreement (external stability), assuming that the remaining players do not revise their membership decision. Following Carraro & Siniscalco, (1993), Hoel (1992), de Zeeuw (2008), it is shown that a stable coalition is formed by few countries if they act in a Cournot vein, in contrast, the size of a stable coalition increases if play - ers act in a Stackelberg fashion (see Barrett, 1994; Diamantoudi & Sartzetakis 2006; Rubio & Ulph 2006).
